prompt: What does a `.metadata.json` file in a `mongodump` directory hold about the collection's indexes?

choices.text: Their definitions
choices.why: Right. The index itself is built again from the documents on every restore.

choices.text: The index files, compressed so the restore can skip building them
choices.why: A few hundred bytes cannot hold an index over 100,000 orders; only the description is there.

choices.text: Nothing: indexes are not part of a dump at all
choices.why: The restore printed `restoring indexes ... from metadata`, so the definitions travel.

choices.text: How many times each index was used since the server started
choices.why: Usage statistics are not backed up; they belong to the running server.

prompt: Why did this lesson's server have to be a replica set, even with one member?

choices.text: Because `mongodump` refuses to connect to a standalone server
choices.why: A plain dump works against a standalone; the option that needs more is `--oplog`.

choices.text: Because `--oplog` reads the oplog, and only a replica-set member keeps one
choices.why: Right. That is the only reason; nothing here needs a second copy.

choices.text: Because a named volume can be mounted only by a replica set
choices.why: Volumes do not care what runs on them; the snapshot copy ran as a standalone.

choices.text: Because MongoDB 8.0 runs every server as a replica set
choices.why: Lesson 1's `mongo` was a standalone server.

prompt: A dump without `--oplog` copied `payments` at 20:15:11.762 and finished `orders` at 20:15:12.073, while writes went on. What is wrong with restoring it as it is?

choices.text: Nothing, because a dump locks the database while it runs
choices.why: The payments kept arriving during the dump; nothing was locked.

choices.text: The orders would be missing their indexes
choices.why: Index definitions travel with or without `--oplog`.

choices.text: Each collection reflects a different moment, so the restore shows a state that never existed
choices.why: Right. `--oplog` and `--oplogReplay` bring every collection to the end of the dump.

choices.text: The archive would be too large to copy out with `docker cp`
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with it; the problem is time.

prompt: To restore a dump taken with `--oplog` to the moment it ended, `mongorestore` is given the option `--___`.
Why was `db.fsyncLock()` run before the `tar` of the volume?

choices.text: So that no file changed while the copy was being made
choices.why: Right. A file-by-file copy of a changing server can be a state that never existed.

choices.text: So that `tar` could read files owned by the `mongodb` user inside the volume
choices.why: The throwaway container ran as root and could read them anyway; the lock is about change.

choices.text: So that the copy would leave the indexes out and come out smaller
choices.why: The snapshot carried the indexes; that is why it was nearly six times the dump.

choices.text: So that clients would be disconnected before the backup
choices.why: Clients stay connected; their writes wait.

prompt: The snapshot archive was 4,687,568 bytes and the dump archive 810,350 bytes. How many times larger is the snapshot? One decimal place.
On a replica set of three, where should the lock and the file copy go, and why?

choices.text: On the primary, since it has the newest data
choices.why: Locking the primary stops every write in the application for the length of the copy.

choices.text: On all three at once, so the copies agree
choices.why: With every member locked nothing can be written, which is the outage this avoids.

choices.text: On a secondary: the primary keeps working and the secondary catches up afterwards
choices.why: Right, from the oplog, once it is unlocked.

choices.text: Nowhere: on a replica set the files can be copied without a lock
choices.why: Each member's files change while it runs, replica set or not.

prompt: The snapshot copy was started without `--replSet`. Why?

choices.text: It names `mongo:27017` as the only member, and the copy is not it
choices.why: Right. Started as a standalone it reads the files, and the log says they belong to a set.

choices.text: A snapshot drops the replica-set configuration, so there is nothing to join
choices.why: The log line shows the configuration is still in the files.

choices.text: A standalone server starts faster
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; identity is.

choices.text: `--replSet` cannot be combined with a named volume
choices.why: The original server used both.

prompt: Match each job to the tool or option in this lesson that does it.
hint: One tool does none of them.

pairs.left: writes documents and index definitions out
brings every collection of a dump to one moment
makes the data files hold still while they are copied

pairs.right: starting a mongod on the files

prompt: A collection of 400 GB with six indexes has to come back within an hour of a disaster. Which backup can promise that, and how would you know?
hint: Which restore does work in proportion to data times indexes?

choices.text: The dump, because it is smaller and copies faster
choices.why: Copying is the cheap half; inserting 400 GB and building six indexes is the expensive one.

choices.text: Either one, since both restored 100,000 orders in about two seconds
choices.why: At 100,000 orders everything is fast; the two scale differently.

choices.text: A snapshot is the likelier one, and only a timed restore of that size settles it
choices.why: Right. The reasoning points at the snapshot; the drill is what makes it a promise.

choices.text: Neither, because MongoDB cannot restore anything above 100 GB
choices.why: There is no such limit; the question is time.

prompt: Why does a `mongodump` taken through `mongos` not represent one moment of the sharded cluster?

choices.text: Each shard is copied at its own pace and there is no single oplog to replay
choices.why: Right, so `--oplog` is not available there.

choices.text: `mongos` caches old documents and returns them during the dump
choices.why: `mongos` stores nothing; it routes.

choices.text: The balancer deletes chunks while they are being dumped
choices.why: Moving data is a separate risk; the main problem is no common moment across shards.

choices.text: The config server refuses reads during a dump
choices.why: It does not; the dump reads it like any other server.

prompt: Which of the two copies keeps the oplog and the journal?

choices.text: The dump, inside its archive
choices.why: The dump keeps only the oplog entries written during the dump, not the server's oplog.

choices.text: The file snapshot
choices.why: Right: it copies everything under `/data/db`.

choices.text: Both, since each restored every collection with every index
choices.why: The dump rebuilt the indexes; it did not carry the server's files.

choices.text: Neither, because those are recreated whenever a server starts
choices.why: The snapshot carried them, which is part of why it was larger.

prompt: After the restore, `payments` held 142 documents and the original 500. What does the gap measure?

choices.text: A restore that failed halfway
choices.why: The log reported 0 failures and every other collection matched.

choices.text: The writes made after the dump ended, which no backup taken then could hold
choices.why: Right. It is what a restore loses, and it says how often backups have to run.

choices.text: Payments the oplog replay applied twice
choices.why: Applying entries cannot leave fewer documents; the restore has fewer, not more.

choices.text: Documents that `mongodump` skipped because the collection was locked while it ran
choices.why: Nothing was locked during the dump.

prompt: Why does the drill restore into a container that has never seen the shop?

choices.text: Because `mongorestore` refuses to write into a database that already exists
choices.why: It writes into existing databases; that is exactly what would hide a broken backup.

choices.text: So nothing already there makes the restore look better than it is
choices.why: Right. A collection already present would pass a check the backup alone would fail.

choices.text: To get a newer MongoDB version
choices.why: Both use `mongo:8.0`.

choices.text: Because the original's volume is still locked
choices.why: It was unlocked right after the copy.

prompt: In what order did `mongorestore --oplogReplay` do its work?

choices.text: Indexes, then documents, then the oplog
choices.why: Building indexes first would make every insert slower; the log shows them last.

choices.text: Documents, then the oplog entries, then the indexes
choices.why: Right: `finished restoring`, `applied 26 oplog entries`, `restoring indexes`.

choices.text: The oplog first, so the documents land already up to date
choices.why: Entries are replayed on top of the documents, so the documents come first.

choices.text: All three at once, one collection at a time
choices.why: The log shows three phases across all collections.

prompt: Put the restore drill in order.
items: Start a server that has never seen the data
Compare counts and indexes against the source
Record the time and every difference
trap: A comparison needs something restored to compare.

prompt: The data of the `mongo` container survives `docker rm` because it lives in a named ___.
Which of these are true of the two backups in this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The dump restore built the indexes from the documents
choices.why: Right: `restoring indexes ... from metadata`.

choices.text: The snapshot was taken while the server kept accepting writes
choices.why: Writes were blocked by `fsyncLock` for the length of the copy.

choices.text: The dump held payments written while it ran, thanks to the oplog
choices.why: Right: 119 copied, 142 after the replay.

choices.text: Either file, kept inside the container, survives `docker rm -f mongo`
choices.why: A file inside a container goes with it; that is why the archive was copied out.

prompt: A team runs `mongodump` every night and has never restored one. What do they actually know?

choices.text: That they can recover from any disaster
choices.why: A backup nobody restored has not shown it can be restored.

choices.text: That a command ran
choices.why: Right, and nothing about whether the data comes back, or how long it takes.

choices.text: How long a restore takes, from the dump's own duration
choices.why: A dump's duration says little about a restore that also builds every index.

choices.text: That their indexes are safe, since the metadata is in the dump
choices.why: Definitions are there; whether they build, and in what time, is untested.

prompt: A shop can afford to lose at most fifteen minutes of orders. What does that decide about its dumps?

choices.text: Each dump has to finish in under fifteen minutes
choices.why: Duration matters less than the gap between one backup and the next.

choices.text: The dumps have to use `--gzip`
choices.why: Compression changes size, not what is lost.

choices.text: Nothing, since `--oplog` already makes a dump lossless
choices.why: It makes a dump consistent at its end; writes after that are still lost.

choices.text: A backup has to complete at least every fifteen minutes
choices.why: Right. What a restore loses is everything written after the last backup ended.

prompt: Why was the snapshot written by a throwaway container rather than by `docker exec` into the server's own container?

choices.text: So the archive lands on the VM, outside the server's container
choices.why: Right. A backup kept inside the container it protects is lost with it.

choices.text: The server's container has no `tar` of its own to make the archive with
choices.why: Both run the same image, `mongo:8.0`, which has `tar`.

choices.text: `docker exec` cannot run inside a container while `fsyncLock` holds its writes
choices.why: `docker exec` ran `fsyncUnlock` while the lock held.

choices.text: A throwaway container copies faster
choices.why: Speed is the same; the point is where the file ends up.

prompt: Why was the archive copied out of the container with `docker cp` right after the dump?

choices.text: To compress it
choices.why: `--gzip` had already compressed it.

choices.text: A backup inside the container it protects is lost with it
choices.why: Right. `docker rm -f mongo` would take the server and its only backup together.

choices.text: Because `mongorestore` can only read archives from the VM's disk, never from a container
choices.why: It ran inside a container, reading `/tmp/shop.archive.gz` there.

choices.text: Because the archive is deleted automatically as soon as the dump finishes
choices.why: It stays where it was written until something removes it.
